summary: This memo describes plans for supporting route aggregation, as used by CIDR and BGP-4, in the NSFNET Policy-Based Routing Database. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This paper explains how the main US research network planned to handle bundled route entries so its lists stayed short. It is historic.

questions: how does nsfnet do route aggregation
subtitle: Supporting route aggregation in NSFNET backbone routing

tldr.problem: The Internet routing table was growing too fast, threatening router performance. Network operators needed a way to combine multiple IP routes into a single aggregate entry to reduce routing table size.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1482 describes how the NSFNET backbone service will accept CIDR-style route aggregates (IP prefixes with prefix length), perform aggregation on behalf of non-CIDR peers, and announce aggregates to neighboring networks. It also proposes a shared registry for tracking aggregate information across the Internet.
tldr.outcome: This specification became the operational model for how Internet backbone networks deployed CIDR and BGP-4 in the mid-1990s, helping manage explosive routing table growth.

today: RFC 1482 is Historic. CIDR and BGP-4 aggregation became the standard way the Internet handles routing. The CIDR Aggregate Registry evolved into modern routing registries and IRRs (Internet Routing Registries) that operators still use today for routing coordination.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
By 1993, the Internet routing table was expanding rapidly as more organizations connected to the network and obtained their own IP address space. The traditional system of assigning address blocks by class (Class A, B, C networks) was inefficient and led to a huge number of individual route entries. Each router had to store and process millions of separate routes.

RFC 1482 describes how the NSFNET backbone service (the primary US research network at the time) planned to implement route aggregation using Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) and BGP-4. The RFC covers the necessary changes to NSFNET's policy-based routing database and proposes a community registry for sharing aggregate information across the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet needed a way to combine many small route entries into bigger bundles so routers wouldn't have to remember millions of separate paths.

sections.title: CIDR and Route Aggregation Basics
sections.content:
CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) represents an IP network as a prefix and a prefix length, using notation like <192.64.128 17>, meaning the first 17 bits match 192.64.128. This allows flexible network sizes, not just the rigid classes of the old system.

Route aggregation combines multiple specific routes into a single aggregate route. For example, if a network provider controls addresses 192.64.128 through 192.64.255, it can announce a single aggregate covering that range instead of 128 separate routes. BGP-4 (Border Gateway Protocol version 4) is the routing protocol that carries these CIDR aggregates between autonomous systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of saying 'here are 100 different routes', a network can say 'everything starting with 192.64 comes to me', which is much simpler.

sections.title: NSFNET Implementation Plan
sections.content:
RFC 1482 describes three ways NSFNET would handle aggregates. First, NSFNET can accept aggregates from regional networks that support BGP-4, treating the prefix as a routing destination. Second, NSFNET can perform aggregation by proxy, where it creates an aggregate on behalf of a non-CIDR peer if certain conditions are met (for example, if smaller routes matching the aggregate are heard, NSFNET announces the aggregate itself).

Third, NSFNET can announce aggregates to neighboring networks using its existing policy mechanisms. The RFC notes an important limitation: NSFNET will not perform de-aggregation (splitting an aggregate back into smaller routes) on outbound announcements, so neighbors must support CIDR or use default routing.
sections.plainLanguage: NSFNET can receive bundles from other networks, create bundles on their behalf, and send bundles to its neighbors.

sections.title: The CIDR Aggregate Registry
sections.content:
RFC 1482 proposes implementing a shared database called the CIDR Aggregate Registry where network providers can register their routes and share aggregate information. Each registry entry records the aggregate itself (the prefix), the home autonomous system (originating AS), announcing autonomous systems, neighbor lists, and administrative contacts.

The registry allows multiple entries for the same aggregate, showing the home AS and each transit AS that announces it. This creates visibility into both route aggregates and Internet topology. Merit proposed to maintain this registry and integrate it with NSFNET's own routing announcements, accepting updates via email and online tools.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared list of all the big route bundles that networks announce, showing who created them and who is passing them on.

sections.title: Operational Impact and Challenges
sections.content:
RFC 1482 discusses significant operational changes required for CIDR deployment. Tools and reports used to configure the network would need updating, and the transition from older routing software (rcp_routed) to new CIDR-capable software (GateD) would be substantial. Network providers had to plan for changes to IP address assignment policies and network renumbering.

The RFC acknowledges unresolved issues: debugging with aggregates (tracing connectivity problems through hidden routes), routing stability under aggregation, and potential network load when packets are sent to aggregates that contain empty address space. Despite these challenges, the community agreed that summer 1993 was the time to enable BGP-4 and CIDR, with each organization responsible for its own implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Using route bundles meant changing how network managers configured everything, and some problems (like debugging broken connections) would become harder.
